spec.topic: Should schools replace traditional report cards with twice-yearly parent-teacher conferences?

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: Welcome to the debate. Should schools replace traditional report cards with twice-yearly parent-teacher conferences? Maeve, make the case.

utterances.speaker: Maeve
utterances.text: Twice-yearly parent-teacher conferences can replace the information provided by traditional report cards. Because teachers can explain a child's progress in detail during those conferences, families get more useful information.

utterances.speaker: Lucia
utterances.text: Many parents keep their children's school papers in a folder at home. That practical habit is worth remembering when we discuss changing the system.

utterances.speaker: Maeve
utterances.text: When teachers explain a child's progress in detail, parents can ask focused follow-up questions. Those questions help parents understand how to support their children at home.

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: So you are saying that twice-yearly parent-teacher conferences provide detailed explanations of a child's progress.

utterances.speaker: Lucia
utterances.text: But replacing report cards would remove a written record that families can revisit after a conference. In other words, replacing report cards would leave families without a lasting account of the teacher's feedback.

utterances.speaker: Maeve
utterances.text: That is why schools should replace traditional report cards with twice-yearly parent-teacher conferences: the focused discussion gives parents practical guidance. The school year contains many difficult conversations for families and teachers.

spec.topic: Should publicly funded research be required to publish all results, including failed experiments?

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Publicly funded research should be required to publish all results, including failed experiments. The reason is simple: taxpayers pay for every experiment, whatever its outcome.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Unpublished failures send other laboratories down the same dead ends, and that repetition wastes public money, which is why hidden failures cost us dearly.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Journals mostly reject negative results. That is why a mandatory public registry matters, since it would remove their power to bury them.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Some will object that writing up every failed experiment would burden researchers with paperwork.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: That objection fails, because a short structured note of a few paragraphs would be enough for a failure.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: I spent two years in a chemistry lab as a student.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Another worry is that some experiments fail only because of faulty equipment and would mislead readers.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A note can record the equipment fault, so readers are not misled.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: There is a further reason to require it: researchers who know their failures will be public design their experiments more carefully. In other words, mandatory publication of failures would improve the quality of research design.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The funder in my country already requires registration of clinical trials.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Public money should buy knowledge that everyone can use, not only the successes.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In short, funding bodies should demand the full record of what they pay for, and publication of all results is exactly that.

utterances.text: Publicly funded research should be required to publish all results, including failed experiments, because taxpayers pay for every experiment, whether it succeeds or fails.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Journals favour positive findings, which is why failed experiments rarely reach print.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The consequence is plain, since other laboratories repeat experiments that have already failed elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Critics say publishing every result would force researchers to spend time writing up work that has no interest to anyone.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: But a short structured note of a few paragraphs per failed experiment would take an hour or two to write.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: I once worked in a laboratory in a converted textile mill.

utterances.speaker: Author

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Failed experiments are as informative as successful ones about what is true.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Put another way, negative results are data that tell the field which paths lead nowhere.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Researchers may fear that publishing failures damages their careers.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: That fear is why funders should count published null results as evidence of rigour when judging grant renewals.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Another reason for the rule is that medical trials that go unpublished have led doctors to prescribe drugs that did not work.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Public archives are cheap to run these days.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: My neighbour is a statistician who dislikes spreadsheets.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: To sum up, a mandatory publication rule is both fair to the public and good for science.

spec.topic: Should criminal trials require unanimous jury verdicts in every serious offence?

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Should criminal trials require unanimous jury verdicts in every serious offence?

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: Serious criminal trials should require unanimous jury verdicts, because unanimity reduces the risk that a defendant will be convicted despite a serious unresolved doubt.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: In other words, Yara's position is that serious criminal trials should require unanimous jury verdicts.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: Because serious trials require unanimity, every juror must be persuaded before a conviction can be returned.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Put another way, the unanimity requirement means that every juror must be persuaded before conviction.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: For context, I once served as a court reporter in a civil case.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: A unanimous rule can expose a weak prosecution case before an unjust conviction occurs, because a single dissenting juror can require the prosecution's evidence to receive additional scrutiny.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: What is the strongest argument against the rule?

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: But requiring unanimity can allow one unreasonable juror to block a justified conviction.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So you are saying that one unreasonable juror could prevent a justified conviction under a unanimous-verdict rule.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: A retrial after a divided jury can protect the public without treating the first trial as proof of guilt, because a divided jury signals that the evidence has not produced sufficient agreement for a final conviction.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: The courthouse café closes at four o'clock.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: Courts should require unanimous verdicts in every serious criminal offence.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: What ultimately justifies imposing that requirement?

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: A unanimous verdict gives the criminal justice system broader public legitimacy, and that is one reason courts should require unanimity in every serious criminal offence.

spec.topic: Should manufacturers be required to sell replacement parts and repair manuals for electronic devices?

utterances.speaker: Enzo
utterances.text: I think manufacturers should be required to sell replacement parts and repair manuals for electronic devices, because repairable devices stay in use for years longer, which cuts the amount of electronic waste.

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: But that would expose their trade secrets, since a repair manual shows how the device is built.

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: Side note: my cousin runs a phone repair stall in the market.

utterances.speaker: Valentina
utterances.text: Xavier, a repair manual only describes how to fix a device, and it does not reveal how it is designed or manufactured, so that objection ignores what a manual is.

utterances.speaker: Enzo
utterances.text: The rule would also mean independent repair shops could get the parts they need. In other words, manufacturers could no longer lock repair work into their own service centres.

utterances.speaker: Valentina
utterances.text: Independent shops already charge much less than manufacturer centres, and cheaper repairs mean people fix devices instead of replacing them.

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: So you are saying that the rule would cut the cost of keeping a device running, Valentina?

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: Anecdotally, my laptop battery lasted six years before it needed replacing.

utterances.speaker: Enzo
utterances.text: The rule would give independent repairers access to parts and information that manufacturers now keep to themselves.

utterances.speaker: Valentina
utterances.text: So the thread leans toward requiring manufacturers to sell parts and manuals.

utterances.text: Managers should be required to advertise vacancies internally before recruiting externally, because that would give current employees a fair chance to apply.

utterances.speaker: Odette
utterances.text: I disagree: external recruitment can bring skills that the organisation currently lacks. On a separate personal note, I changed my train route this morning.

utterances.speaker: Matteo
utterances.text: Internal advertising can reveal qualified employees whom managers might otherwise overlook. That is why current employees deserve a fair chance to apply.

utterances.speaker: Matteo
utterances.text: A seven-day internal posting is sufficient for most vacancies, so an internal posting would add little time to most recruitment processes; that is another reason to require it.

utterances.speaker: Matteo
utterances.text: Internal candidates already understand the organisation's systems and procedures. The human-resources calendar is busiest in June.

utterances.speaker: Odette
utterances.text: But a mandatory internal posting could delay urgent appointments.

utterances.speaker: Matteo
utterances.text: That objection has an answer: an emergency exception would prevent urgent appointments from being delayed, which is why the requirement would remain workable.

utterances.speaker: Odette
utterances.text: So you are saying that internal advertising gives current employees a fair chance to apply.

utterances.speaker: Matteo
utterances.text: In other words, your position is that external recruitment supplies skills the organisation lacks.

utterances.speaker: Matteo
utterances.text: Put another way, my proposal would make internal advertising mandatory before external recruitment.

utterances.speaker: Matteo
utterances.text: That is to say, your concern is that mandatory internal advertising could delay urgent appointments.

spec.topic: Should planning rules require every new home to include a rainwater-collection system?

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Planning rules should require every new home to include a rainwater-collection system. Summers in this region are getting drier, which is reason enough.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Fitting a tank while a house is being built costs far less than adding one later, and that is a further reason for the rule. Put another way, retrofitting a finished home is far more expensive.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Builders object that a mandatory tank would add too much to the price of new homes. In other words, the rule would price some buyers out.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: But the extra cost is repaid through lower water bills, and that is one more reason to make the rule universal.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A tank cuts a household's mains water use by about a third, which is why the bills fall and a further reason for the rule.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: My own water butt filled in a single night last March.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The council votes on its local plan next month.

spec.topic: Should mobile operating systems be required to allow alternative app stores?

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight's question: should phone operating systems be forced to allow alternative app stores? Florin, you first.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: Yes, they should, because a single official store lets the platform owner charge developers up to thirty percent commission on every sale.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Rashid, you disagree?

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: But alternative stores would make phones less safe. I say that as someone who works in payment security.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So, Rashid, you are saying that opening up the platform costs users their safety. Ulla?

utterances.speaker: Ulla
utterances.text: Developers currently have no other route to reach phone users, which is another reason to open it up. Incidentally, the Brussels hearing on this ran for six hours.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: Put another way, developers are locked in to a single store.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Rashid, what protects users today?

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: The official store's review process is the main protection they have, since it blocks thousands of malicious apps a year.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Florin, what about the effect on fees?

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: Rival stores would push fees down, because fees on desktop game stores fell once rivals appeared.

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: In other words, you want the platform owner to lose its toll on every sale.

utterances.speaker: Ulla
utterances.text: Higher commissions get passed on to consumers as higher app prices, since subscription prices rose in the months after the last fee increase.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: Several developers have said publicly that they raised prices because of the commission, which bears out Ulla's point.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Thank you all. That is all we have time for tonight.

spec.topic: Should governments cap the fees charged by payment-processing companies to small businesses?

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight's question: should governments cap the fees payment processors charge small businesses? Pradeep, you first.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: Yes, a cap is needed, because a typical café hands over about three percent of every card sale, which is most of its profit margin.

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: But a cap would backfire, because processors would simply add monthly charges to make up the lost income.

utterances.speaker: Olumide
utterances.text: So what you mean is that the money would just come back through other fees. Incidentally, I ran a bakery for six years.

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: Yes, and they would, since their fraud and network costs are fixed and cannot be absorbed.

utterances.speaker: Olumide
utterances.text: Europe's interchange cap shows that caps can work: merchants' costs fell by about a third afterwards.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Pradeep, what about the smallest shops?

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: Small shops pay nearly double what supermarkets pay for the same card transaction, which is why the current fee structure is unfair.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: And how do they cope with that?

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: Many of them cannot afford to turn down cards, yet they struggle to afford the fees.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So, Pradeep, you are saying small shops are trapped: they must accept cards but struggle to pay for them.

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: A cap would also force the smaller processors out of the market. The sector employs about forty thousand people here.

utterances.speaker: Olumide
utterances.text: So you are saying that a cap would leave only the big processors standing.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Thank you all. We will leave it there.

utterances.text: Welcome to the debate. Should pharmacies be allowed to prescribe routine antibiotics for minor infections without a doctor's appointment?

utterances.speaker: Hamza
utterances.text: The debate is being broadcast from Studio 4.

utterances.speaker: Imogen
utterances.text: I arrived before the cameras went live.

utterances.speaker: Thandiwe
utterances.text: Hamza, why do you support the proposal?

utterances.speaker: Hamza
utterances.text: Pharmacies should be allowed to prescribe routine antibiotics for minor infections without a doctor's appointment because pharmacists can identify many minor infections using approved screening protocols.

utterances.speaker: Hamza

utterances.speaker: Imogen

utterances.speaker: Imogen
utterances.text: The proposed service would make antibiotics easier for patients to obtain. Because that increased convenience could encourage people to seek antibiotics for viral illnesses, it could increase unnecessary use.

utterances.speaker: Enzo
utterances.text: Since allowing pharmacists to handle minor infections would give local clinics more time for complex patients, the policy would improve access to medical care.

utterances.speaker: Hamza

spec.topic: Should banks be allowed to use facial recognition instead of passwords for customer authentication?

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Esther, should banks be allowed to replace passwords with facial recognition?

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: Yes, they should be allowed, because passwords are routinely stolen in phishing attacks.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Does the face then replace everything else?

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: I would also back it since customers reuse one password across many sites. For large transfers the scan would sit beside a one-time code.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So you are saying the face would be one factor among several.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: Critics say a stolen face cannot be reset the way a password can, but a breach would reveal nothing usable.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Why would nothing usable leak?

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: Because banks would keep only encrypted templates on the customer's device.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: In other words, the template is useless to a thief.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: Exactly. My own bank already lets me log in with my fingerprint.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: What about accuracy across different groups of people?

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: Error rates differ between demographic groups in some systems, so banks must test for that before launch.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: And for those the scanner fails?

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: They should keep a password fallback, because no scanner works for everyone.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Put another way, nobody should be forced onto face scanning.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: Live-face checks block photo spoofing, and that alone justifies allowing the technology. Banks that skip testing would also lose their customers' trust, hence testing is non-negotiable.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: I read that three banks in the region trialled it last year. Thank you, Esther.

utterances.speaker: Lorenzo
utterances.text: Welcome to the programme. Tonight's question: should national elections switch to proportional representation? Zainab, you first.

utterances.speaker: Zainab
utterances.text: Yes, we should switch. The reason is that under constituency voting a party can win a majority of seats with well under half of the votes.

utterances.speaker: Meera
utterances.text: But proportional representation severs the link between an MP and a local area.

utterances.speaker: Abena
utterances.text: Exactly, because under proportional representation voters lose control over who gets elected.

utterances.speaker: Meera
utterances.text: That is the reason, yes: party leaders set the order of candidates on the lists.

utterances.speaker: Lorenzo
utterances.text: So, Meera, you are saying proportional representation weakens the tie between MPs and their areas.

utterances.speaker: Seamus
utterances.text: I have lived in the same constituency for thirty years. Single-member constituencies give stable single-party governments.

utterances.speaker: Seamus
utterances.text: That matters because stable governments can pass long-term policy.

utterances.speaker: Lorenzo
utterances.text: So you are saying, Seamus, that constituency voting produces clear single-party governments.

utterances.speaker: Zainab
utterances.text: Look at the last election: the winning party took 62 percent of seats on 38 percent of votes, which shows how far a winner can be from majority support.

utterances.speaker: Abena
utterances.text: Turnout is lowest in safe seats, which shows that many votes under the constituency system count for nothing.

utterances.speaker: Zainab
utterances.text: In other words, the constituency system leaves millions of voters without any representation.

utterances.speaker: Meera
utterances.text: By the way, the next election is due in May.

spec.topic: Should police be required to livestream all custodial interrogations?

utterances.speaker: Malik
utterances.text: Police should be required to livestream every custodial interrogation. The reason is that livestreaming every custodial interrogation would create an immediate public record of police questioning.

utterances.speaker: Agnieszka
utterances.text: Recorded interrogations make disputed accounts checkable, because a complete recording preserves the exact questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: Malik
utterances.text: That checkability helps courts assess whether questioning was coercive.

utterances.speaker: Alina
utterances.text: So you are saying that police should be required to livestream every custodial interrogation.

utterances.speaker: Agnieszka
utterances.text: But requiring a livestream of every custodial interrogation would expose sensitive victims and witnesses.

utterances.speaker: Malik
utterances.text: The forum's banner was redesigned last week.

utterances.speaker: Malik
utterances.text: Recordings protect officers from false allegations, because an objective record can rebut inaccurate accusations against officers.

utterances.speaker: Alina
utterances.text: Courts can identify coercive questioning more reliably when they can review the interrogation record, which gives defendants a stronger basis for challenging coercive questioning.

utterances.speaker: Agnieszka
utterances.text: In other words, a reviewable interrogation record gives defendants stronger grounds to challenge coercive questioning.

utterances.speaker: Malik
utterances.text: Since that protection depends on an objective account of the interrogation, a recording that protects officers depends on an objective account of the interrogation.

utterances.speaker: Alina
utterances.text: Put another way, officer protection from false allegations requires an objective interrogation account.

utterances.speaker: Alina
utterances.text: I prefer discussions that include links to primary documents.

utterances.speaker: Malik
utterances.text: Because an objective interrogation account can be independently reviewed, independent review of an objective interrogation account can identify coercive questioning. That identification can deter coercive police practices.

utterances.speaker: Alina
utterances.text: In other words, independent review of interrogation footage can discourage coercive police practices.

spec.topic: Should secondary schools require every student to complete a financial-literacy course before graduating?

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Matteo, you want financial literacy made compulsory. Why?

utterances.speaker: Matteo
utterances.text: Every secondary school should require a financial-literacy course before graduation, because many school leavers sign credit agreements without understanding interest.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: What makes them so exposed?

utterances.speaker: Matteo
utterances.text: Credit card companies target eighteen-year-olds with aggressive offers, which is why so many sign blindly. And a course would give students the habit of budgeting before they start earning, which is a second reason to require it.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Some teachers argue a required course would squeeze out other subjects.

utterances.speaker: Matteo
utterances.text: That ignores that one period a week for one semester is enough, which is one more reason to make it required. Pilot schools fitted such a course into the existing timetable without dropping any subject.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So you are saying the course takes up little timetable space.

utterances.speaker: Matteo
utterances.text: Yes, and fewer than half of adults can answer a basic question about inflation, which is another reason to start in school. Incidentally, my school in Bologna runs until five in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: How should it be assessed?

utterances.speaker: Matteo
utterances.text: With simulations rather than exams, since students retain practical skills better when they practise them in class.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: In other words, for money skills, learning by doing beats memorising?

utterances.speaker: Matteo
utterances.text: My own teacher ran a budgeting unit and I still use the method.

spec.topic: Should voting be compulsory, with a modest penalty for eligible citizens who abstain without justification?

utterances.speaker: Jolene
utterances.text: Item two: should we back compulsory voting, with a modest fine for people who abstain without a good reason? Kai, would you start?

utterances.speaker: Kai
utterances.text: We should back compulsory voting with a modest fine, because turnout in local elections has fallen to about thirty percent.

utterances.speaker: Babajide
utterances.text: But compulsory voting infringes individual freedom, since someone who dislikes every candidate would be forced to pick one.

utterances.speaker: Kai
utterances.text: Last May only four thousand of thirteen thousand registered voters turned out, which shows how low turnout has fallen.

utterances.speaker: Jolene
utterances.text: How big would the fine need to be?

utterances.speaker: Kai
utterances.text: A fine of around twenty dollars is a nudge rather than coercion, because in Australia the fine is about that and turnout stays above ninety percent.

utterances.speaker: Jolene
utterances.text: In other words, a small fine only gently pushes people to the polls. Also, the hall is booked until five o'clock.

utterances.speaker: Babajide
utterances.text: Fines fall hardest on poorer voters, because low-income workers often cannot leave their shifts to vote.

utterances.speaker: Kai
utterances.text: I have worked at a polling station for ten years.

utterances.speaker: Babajide
utterances.text: I would rather see the effort go into making voting easier.

utterances.speaker: Kai

spec.topic: Should public transport authorities use facial recognition to identify fare evaders?

utterances.speaker: Meera
utterances.text: Tonight we are asking whether public transport authorities should use facial recognition to identify fare evaders. Aurelio, why do you support the idea?

utterances.speaker: Aurelio
utterances.text: Fare inspectors cannot check every passenger who boards a bus or train. Because inspectors cannot check everyone, manual inspections therefore miss some fare evaders.

utterances.speaker: Aurelio
utterances.text: Since manual inspections miss some evaders, facial recognition could flag many of those people.

utterances.speaker: Meera
utterances.text: So, Aurelio's claim is that facial recognition could flag many fare evaders whom manual inspections miss. Priya, does that make the system worthwhile?

utterances.speaker: Priya
utterances.text: I am not persuaded. But facial recognition cannot reliably flag fare evaders because it misidentifies some passengers, and misidentified passengers can receive unjust fare penalties.

utterances.speaker: Meera
utterances.text: Aurelio, Priya has raised both accuracy and fairness concerns. What is your response?

utterances.speaker: Aurelio
utterances.text: A pilot could limit the system to alerts rather than automatic fines, and trained staff could review each alert.

utterances.speaker: Priya
utterances.text: Biometric travel records could reveal where individual passengers regularly go. In other words, facial recognition would create detailed records of passengers' movements.

utterances.speaker: Meera
utterances.text: The privacy issue is clear. We also have an audience question about the scale of the network.

utterances.speaker: Aurelio
utterances.text: The metro's busiest line carries more than 200,000 passengers on a typical weekday.

utterances.speaker: Priya
utterances.text: Random inspections and contactless audits can reduce fare evasion without biometric identification.

utterances.speaker: Meera
utterances.text: The authority plans to replace its ticket machines next spring. Priya, give us your final recommendation.

utterances.speaker: Priya
utterances.text: For those two reasons—the detailed movement records and the availability of non-biometric alternatives—the public transport authority should reject facial recognition for identifying fare evaders.

utterances.speaker: Host

utterances.speaker: Rohan

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: Yes. Sixteen-year-olds should be allowed to vote in local elections if they complete a short civic-education course.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Why should their age not prevent them from voting?

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: Because sixteen-year-olds are directly affected by decisions made by local councils.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: What kinds of decisions do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: Local councils make decisions about schools, transport, and recreational facilities. Those decisions affect young residents every day.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: What is the strongest argument against your position?

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: Critics object that sixteen-year-olds may lack enough civic knowledge for local voting.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Does that objection change your view?

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: It does not defeat the proposal, because that knowledge concern is a serious reason to provide civic education before voting.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So the education requirement is central to your answer?

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: Exactly. In other words, providing civic education before voting is a serious response to the knowledge concern.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: And what is your final position?

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: Therefore, sixteen-year-olds should be allowed to vote after completing civic education. Put another way, I support allowing sixteen-year-olds to vote with that preparation in place.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Did you vote when you were younger?

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: I first voted in a school council election at the age of fourteen.

utterances.text: The interview is taking place on a weekday afternoon.

spec.topic: Should schools abolish class rankings to reduce unhealthy competition among students?

utterances.speaker: Amir
utterances.text: Our question tonight is whether schools should abolish class rankings to reduce unhealthy competition among students. Leilani, you support abolition.

utterances.speaker: Leilani
utterances.text: Schools should abolish class rankings to reduce unhealthy competition among students. At my school, rankings were posted on a corridor noticeboard.

utterances.speaker: Rohan
utterances.text: Schools should retain class rankings because they give students a clear measure of their academic progress.

utterances.speaker: Amara
utterances.text: Students compare their class positions constantly when rankings are public; because of that comparison, learning becomes a contest for status.

utterances.speaker: Amir
utterances.text: Rohan says rankings provide useful information, while Amara says they change the atmosphere of learning. Leilani, what would replace them?

utterances.speaker: Leilani
utterances.text: I volunteer at an after-school music club, where students cooperate rather than compete.

utterances.speaker: Amir
utterances.text: So you are saying that schools should abolish class rankings to reduce unhealthy competition among students?

utterances.speaker: Amara
utterances.text: Yes. Since status competition turns learning into a contest for status, anxious students avoid difficult subjects, which shows that abolishing class rankings is necessary to reduce that anxiety.

utterances.speaker: Rohan
utterances.text: That conclusion overlooks the fact that class rankings help teachers identify students who need academic support.

utterances.speaker: Leilani
utterances.text: Schools can replace public rankings with private feedback on individual progress. Teachers can still discuss weaknesses with each student without publishing a competitive table.

utterances.speaker: Amir
utterances.text: So you are proposing private feedback on individual progress instead of public class rankings.

utterances.speaker: Amara
utterances.text: A pilot at three schools found that private feedback reduced reported rivalry among students.

utterances.speaker: Leilani
utterances.text: For those reasons, including the anxiety evidence and the pilot results, the national school system should abolish class rankings.

spec.topic: Should election day become a public holiday?

utterances.speaker: Bernard
utterances.text: I think election day should become a public holiday. Because a public holiday would give most employees paid time to vote, the change would make participation more accessible.

utterances.speaker: Marisol
utterances.text: The national election authority publishes polling-station staffing rosters six months in advance. Since those rosters are prepared six months ahead, election-day planning is predictable.

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: I disagree with the proposal for this reason: making election day a public holiday would not by itself increase turnout.

utterances.speaker: Marisol
utterances.text: In other words, a public holiday would not automatically bring more voters to the polls. Many voters already have flexible evening or early-voting options, which is why the holiday alone may have little effect.

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: A public holiday would make voting easier for people who work irregular shifts. But that improvement would not remove all barriers to voting.

utterances.speaker: Bernard
utterances.text: Many polling places do not provide childcare, and because of that limitation, easier scheduling would not solve every access problem.

utterances.speaker: Marisol
utterances.text: As a side note, the central library has extended its weekend opening hours.

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: The election authority's budget includes a contingency for temporary staff. That reserve matters because it gives the authority money for staffing changes.

utterances.speaker: Marisol
utterances.text: So you are saying that the election authority could use its contingency budget to cover extra temporary staff. Because that contingency exists, staffing costs should not defeat the proposal for a public holiday.

utterances.speaker: Bernard
utterances.text: Put another way, the cost of extra election-day staff should not be a reason to reject a public holiday.

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: A paid day off would give many voters time to reach a polling station. That practical opportunity is one reason I support the change.

utterances.speaker: Marisol
utterances.text: Countries with holiday elections often report high voter participation. In other words, holiday elections are frequently associated with strong participation.

utterances.speaker: Bernard
utterances.text: I usually vote early by mail, although that is only my personal habit.

utterances.speaker: Bernard
utterances.text: For these reasons, Parliament should make election day a public holiday: a paid day off would give voters time to reach polling stations, staffing costs should not defeat the plan, and countries with holiday elections often report strong participation.

utterances.speaker: Bernard
utterances.text: Many hourly workers cannot vote during ordinary work hours. Because of that barrier, a public holiday on election day would remove a major scheduling obstacle to voting.

utterances.speaker: Marisol
utterances.text: Removing that scheduling barrier would enable more workers to vote, because people would not have to choose between their wages and the ballot.

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: So you are saying that a public holiday would broaden access to voting for workers. I understand the appeal, but access is not the only issue.

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: Election offices already face staffing shortages. That means a public holiday could make election administration harder.

utterances.speaker: Bernard
utterances.text: In other words, election offices could have difficulty operating on a public holiday. That practical risk is a serious concern, but it does not settle the question.

utterances.speaker: Marisol
utterances.text: Employers would still have to pay many workers who receive holiday leave, so making election day a public holiday would impose additional wage costs on employers.

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: Countries with holiday elections often report higher voter turnout. That evidence supports the view that a holiday can increase turnout.

utterances.speaker: Marisol
utterances.text: A public holiday could also make voting feel like a shared civic event.

utterances.speaker: Bernard
utterances.text: Put another way, a public holiday could give voting a stronger collective character.

utterances.speaker: Marisol
utterances.text: The legal change needed for a public holiday is procedurally straightforward.

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: That is to say, the required legal amendment would be relatively simple to pass. Because the amendment would be straightforward, it would give Parliament a clear route to creating the holiday.

utterances.speaker: Bernard
utterances.text: A clear legislative route would allow Parliament to establish the holiday without changing the voting system.

utterances.speaker: Bernard
utterances.text: As a personal aside, I prefer coffee to tea during these forum discussions.

utterances.speaker: Marisol
utterances.text: Unrelated note: I plan to attend a concert next month.

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: Taking the accessibility and legislative points together, election day should become a public holiday.

utterances.speaker: Chidi
utterances.text: Tonight we are asking whether councils should give residents a direct say over a fixed share of the annual budget. Dolores, you support the proposal?

utterances.speaker: Dolores
utterances.text: I do support it because residents often know which local improvements are most urgently needed. Councils should allow residents to vote directly on how a fixed portion of the annual budget is spent.

utterances.speaker: Gabriela
utterances.text: But direct budget votes can give disproportionate influence to well-organised neighbourhood groups. The objection, in other words, is that direct budget votes can give disproportionate influence to well-organised neighbourhood groups.

utterances.speaker: Chidi
utterances.text: Gabriela, does limiting the amount of money settle that concern?

utterances.speaker: Gabriela
utterances.text: Councils could limit the scheme to ten percent of the annual budget. A ten-percent limit would protect spending on essential services, because the vote could not reach the money needed for core obligations.

utterances.speaker: Dolores
utterances.text: Carefully designed public meetings can help quieter residents participate. Trained facilitators can give less confident residents time to present their priorities, which is why those meetings matter.

utterances.speaker: Chidi
utterances.text: So you are saying that public meetings can help quieter residents participate?

utterances.speaker: Dolores
utterances.text: Yes, and a limited pilot would reveal whether residents can use the voting process responsibly. That pilot would expose problems with turnout and administration, which is why testing the process first is sensible.

utterances.speaker: Gabriela
utterances.text: Councils should publish cost estimates for every project on the ballot. Transparent cost estimates would help voters compare competing projects.

utterances.speaker: Chidi
utterances.text: A pilot would make a bounded scheme more defensible because it would reveal whether the process works in practice. In other words, councils should allow residents to make bounded direct decisions about part of the annual budget.

utterances.speaker: Chidi
utterances.text: That concludes this segment; the next item on the programme concerns regional bus services.

utterances.text: Tonight's question: once children type fluently, should primary schools still teach handwriting? Siobhan, you first.

utterances.speaker: Siobhan
utterances.text: Handwriting should stay in the primary curriculum, because children who write by hand remember lessons better.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tobias, where do you stand?

utterances.speaker: Tobias

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Bilal, you teach seven-year-olds.

utterances.speaker: Bilal
utterances.text: Children who struggle with pencil grip often struggle with spelling too, which shows that handwriting builds skills that support spelling.

utterances.speaker: Siobhan
utterances.text: Put another way, writing by hand trains the brain for language, since scans show that more brain regions light up when children write by hand.

utterances.speaker: Tobias
utterances.text: Our school bought tablets for every pupil last year, for what it is worth.

utterances.speaker: Tobias

utterances.speaker: Host

utterances.text: But a typed paragraph often holds less thought than a short handwritten one, because children who type tend to send their work without rereading it.

utterances.speaker: Host

spec.topic: Should professional basketball teams be required to disclose players’ injury details before every game?

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Professional basketball teams should be required to disclose game-relevant injury information before every game without publishing private medical histories. Fans need reliable information about players' availability before games, which is why the requirement is justified.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A player's injury status can materially change the competitive balance of a game. Because that status can change a game's competitive balance, fans need timely information about it.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Players have a legitimate interest in keeping their medical histories private. For that reason, only game-relevant injury status, rather than diagnosis or treatment details, should be disclosed; this narrow scope supports the requirement.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The disclosure rule would be limited to game-relevant status and would exclude medical histories. In other words, the rule should report only information relevant to a player's availability.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Official basketball game-day reports already use categories such as available, questionable, and out. Those existing categories show that useful disclosure can be standardized.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: However, mandatory injury reports could help opponents target vulnerable players, and that risk is a serious objection to requiring disclosure.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The policy could create a competitive safety risk for injured players. Put another way, mandatory reports may expose injured players to competitive disadvantages.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Because official reports use standardized availability categories, fans can receive useful information without seeing medical histories.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The essay was drafted on a rainy Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The author prefers wooden pencils to mechanical pencils.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In short, the proposal is mandatory pregame disclosure of game-relevant injury information rather than full medical records.

spec.topic: Should employers be allowed to monitor workers’ keystrokes and mouse movements?

utterances.speaker: Deirdre

utterances.text: Employers should be allowed to monitor workers' keystrokes and mouse movements while managing remote teams, because keystroke and mouse records can show whether a remote worker is active during paid hours.

spec.topic: Should gene editing be permitted to prevent inherited diseases in human embryos?

utterances.speaker: Zofia
utterances.text: The agenda item is whether gene editing should be permitted to prevent inherited diseases in human embryos. I would like each of us to address both the possible benefits and the safeguards.

utterances.speaker: Zofia
utterances.text: A tightly regulated embryo gene-editing program could prevent some inherited diseases.

utterances.speaker: Efua
utterances.text: Because that possibility is real, embryo gene editing to prevent inherited diseases should be considered by lawmakers.

utterances.speaker: Orla
utterances.text: Since a tightly regulated program could prevent some inherited diseases, a public consultation on embryo gene editing is necessary.

utterances.speaker: Zofia
utterances.text: The same possibility is why any permitted embryo gene-editing procedure would require strict safety standards.

utterances.speaker: Efua
utterances.text: Because a regulated program could prevent some inherited diseases, parents at high risk of transmitting a serious inherited disease should have access to carefully regulated embryo gene editing.

utterances.speaker: Orla
utterances.text: That potential to prevent disease is also why a ban on embryo gene editing would leave some serious inherited diseases preventable in principle but unavoidable in practice.

utterances.speaker: Zofia
utterances.text: Given that disease prevention is the relevant potential benefit, the permission debate should distinguish disease prevention from attempts to enhance preferred traits.

utterances.speaker: Efua
utterances.text: My main concern is that embryo gene editing could create unintended genetic changes.

utterances.speaker: Orla
utterances.text: Because embryo gene editing could create unintended genetic changes, embryo gene editing should not be authorized until long-term safety evidence is available.

utterances.speaker: Zofia
utterances.text: I take an even stronger position: no use of human embryo gene editing can be ethically justified.

utterances.speaker: Efua
utterances.text: But that absolute ethical judgment is too broad because carefully regulated disease prevention could be ethically justified.

utterances.speaker: Orla
utterances.text: A permitted program must prohibit embryo gene editing for cosmetic or enhancement purposes.

utterances.speaker: Zofia
utterances.text: So you are saying that any permitted program must ban embryo gene editing for cosmetic or enhancement purposes.

utterances.speaker: Efua
utterances.text: Independent international review should oversee every proposed clinical use of embryo gene editing.

utterances.speaker: Orla
utterances.text: You mean that every proposed clinical use needs oversight from an independent international body.

utterances.speaker: Zofia
utterances.text: Permission should be limited to preventing serious inherited diseases for which no safe alternative exists.

utterances.speaker: Efua
utterances.text: In other words, permission should cover only serious inherited diseases without a safe alternative treatment.

utterances.speaker: Orla
utterances.text: The national regulator issued revised consent forms last month.

utterances.speaker: Zofia
utterances.text: Several committee members have requested a separate briefing on laboratory funding.

utterances.speaker: Orla
utterances.text: We have identified possible benefits, serious risks, and several conditions for any future permission. The secretary will record these points for the next agenda.

spec.topic: Should retailers pay a levy on unnecessary plastic packaging around fresh produce?

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Should retailers pay a levy on unnecessary plastic packaging around fresh produce?

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: Retailers should pay a levy on unnecessary plastic packaging around fresh produce, because that packaging shifts disposal costs from retailers to local councils.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Why do you regard the levy as fair rather than simply punitive?

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: The levy is fair because retailers choose whether to use unnecessary plastic packaging. A well-designed levy would encourage retailers to use simpler packaging, since simpler packaging would cost less to collect and process.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Some retailers argue that any charge on packaging will hurt smaller businesses.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: Retailers should not pay a levy on any plastic packaging around fresh produce. Small shops need an exemption because they often lack practical alternatives to plastic packaging.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: Fresh produce employs thousands of workers across the country.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Would the levy amount to a ban on plastic packaging?

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: The government can introduce the levy without banning all plastic packaging. A transition period is needed because retailers require time to change their packaging contracts.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: Retailers can replace much unnecessary plastic packaging with paper or reusable containers, because several major suppliers now offer paper and reusable alternatives.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Can you specify which packaging would actually be charged?

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: The levy would apply only when fresh produce is wrapped without a protective or hygiene-related need.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So you are saying the levy would target packaging with no protective or hygiene function rather than all packaging?

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: Retailers could avoid the charge by removing unnecessary wrapping or choosing an alternative material.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: In other words, retailers would have a choice between removing unnecessary wrapping and paying the levy.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: Packaging that is legally required should be exempt from the levy; in other words, retailers should not pay a levy on any plastic packaging that they must use by law.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Put another way, the levy could be introduced without banning every plastic package used for fresh produce?

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: I have advised two grocery chains on reducing their packaging waste.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The charge reduces the number of cars entering the centre at peak times, and that is the main reason to adopt it. Buses through the centre become quicker too, because the charge keeps those cars out.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: I have lived beside the market square for twelve years.

utterances.speaker: Author

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Put differently, drivers should pay for the scarce road space they use at the busiest times. Free peak-time access is therefore a hidden subsidy to car users, because of exactly that.

utterances.text: Stockholm introduced its congestion charge in 2007.

utterances.speaker: Quentin
utterances.text: Our question is whether governments should automatically register citizens who are eligible to vote. Beatriz, you support the proposal.

utterances.speaker: Beatriz
utterances.text: Governments should automatically register eligible citizens to vote, because many eligible citizens are currently missing from electoral rolls.

utterances.speaker: Alina
utterances.text: A second reason to adopt the policy is that automatic registration would reduce the administrative work required to add eligible citizens to electoral rolls. I have voted in every national election since 2008.

utterances.speaker: Carmen
utterances.text: The proposal deserves adoption because automatic registration would make electoral rolls more accurate. I volunteer at a community library on Saturdays.

utterances.speaker: Rania
utterances.text: But automatic registration can leave outdated addresses on the electoral roll; that is an objection to adopting the proposal. A second objection is that automatic registration can register citizens without their active consent.

utterances.speaker: Quentin
utterances.text: Rania has raised concerns about accuracy and consent. Beatriz, how do you answer those concerns?

utterances.speaker: Beatriz
utterances.text: So you are saying that governments should automatically add eligible citizens to the electoral roll. I still think that is the right policy.

utterances.speaker: Alina
utterances.text: The proposed electoral register would be reviewed every five years. That is another reason to adopt automatic registration: citizens could correct their registration details through an online portal.

utterances.speaker: Carmen
utterances.text: The policy should be adopted because automatic registration would make it easier for eligible citizens to participate in elections.

utterances.speaker: Rania
utterances.text: A further reason to adopt the policy is that automatic registration would give citizens more equal access to the voting process. The electoral register's eligibility data would be reviewed on a five-year schedule.

utterances.speaker: Carmen
utterances.text: To put Alina's point another way, the proposed electoral register would undergo review every five years. Separately, the proposed electoral register would be stored in a national database.

utterances.speaker: Rania
utterances.text: In other words, the proposed electoral register would use a national database for storage. The electoral register's eligibility data would be reviewed on a five-year schedule.

utterances.speaker: Quentin
utterances.text: To restate Rania's point, eligibility data on the electoral register would be reviewed every five years.

utterances.speaker: Beatriz
utterances.text: Automatic registration would not legally require anyone to cast a ballot.

utterances.speaker: Alina
utterances.text: Put another way, automatic registration would not compel anyone to vote.

spec.topic: Should amateur boxing replace winning by knockout with points-only scoring?

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: Amateur boxing should replace knockout victories with points-only scoring. The reason is that knockout-focused rules expose amateur boxers to incentives for avoidable head trauma.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: I disagree with that proposal. But knockout victories are legitimate evidence of superiority.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: Unrelated note: my local gym recently replaced several heavy bags.

utterances.speaker: Giulia
utterances.text: To put Bongani's proposal another way, amateur boxing would award wins only through points rather than knockouts.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: A further reason for the replacement is that points-only scoring would let a referee stop a bout for safety without making the stoppage a knockout victory.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: In other words, my objection is that knockout victories are legitimate evidence of superiority.

utterances.speaker: Giulia
utterances.text: The reason I favour the replacement is that points-only scoring rewards sustained technique rather than one decisive blow.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: Another reason for the replacement is that judges can decide a bout on points after a referee stops it for safety.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: So you are saying, in other words, that points-only scoring rewards sustained technique rather than one decisive blow.

utterances.speaker: Giulia
utterances.text: A points decision gives a losing boxer a clearer record of which skills need improvement, which is another reason to adopt the replacement.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: A further reason to adopt the replacement is that removing knockout wins would make early defensive tactics more valuable.

utterances.speaker: Giulia
utterances.text: The replacement is practical because amateur tournaments could use points-only scoring without changing round lengths.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: The forum software logged me out twice today.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: One final reason for the replacement is that points-only scoring would make bout outcomes less dependent on one lucky punch.

utterances.text: So you are saying that the concern about officials ignoring injured boxers under points-only scoring is weak.

spec.topic: Should schools make swimming proficiency a requirement for joining competitive sports teams?

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Should schools make swimming proficiency a requirement for joining competitive sports teams?

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: I would support that requirement because competitive sports teams can expose students to water-related risks during competitions and training.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Some parents worry that such a rule would be unfair to beginners. How do you respond?

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: But requiring proficiency before team membership could exclude students who have had fewer opportunities to learn swimming. The school calendar contains two examination weeks in May.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Would an alternative protect safety without excluding those students?

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: A fairer policy is to let students join teams provisionally while they complete swimming training. Schools can provide swimming lessons for students who do not yet meet the proficiency standard, because that gives them a realistic route onto the team.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Does a proficiency test solve the whole safety problem?

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: No, passing a swimming test would not guarantee that a student would behave safely around water. I learned to swim at age nine.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So you still support swimming proficiency as a condition for joining a competitive team?

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: Yes, in other words, I support making swimming proficiency a condition for joining competitive sports teams.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: What would your training-first version involve?

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: Put another way, my proposed policy would allow students to train before they receive full team membership. Teams can reserve pool time for students who need swimming training, which is why the policy is practical. A basic supervised swimming test is inexpensive for schools to administer, so schools can use proficiency as a condition for full team membership.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: What is the strongest reason for keeping the requirement?

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: Another reason is that students who cannot yet swim may panic if an athletic activity unexpectedly involves deep water. Several local schools already combine sports-team participation with swimming instruction, which shows that a training-first policy can work.

utterances.speaker: Rafael
utterances.text: The same three clubs won eight of ten championships in the last decade, which shows exactly that and is another reason to cap.

utterances.speaker: Ivana

utterances.speaker: Bernard
utterances.text: So you are saying the federation should limit what every club may pay its players.

utterances.speaker: Rafael
utterances.text: Yes. Caps also protect clubs from bankruptcy, since wages swallow most of a club's revenue.

utterances.speaker: Ivana
utterances.text: Put another way, Rafael, a cap is a safety net for clubs against insolvency.

utterances.speaker: Host

spec.topic: Should people be expected to return online purchases to physical shops?

utterances.speaker: Harriet
utterances.text: Welcome to tonight's debate. Should people be expected to return online purchases to physical shops?

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: Yes. People should be expected to return online purchases to physical shops.

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: That expectation is sensible because returning online purchases to physical shops would consolidate parcels and reduce delivery mileage.

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: That reduction follows because physical shops can send several returned parcels together instead of having each parcel collected separately.

utterances.speaker: Malik
utterances.text: A second reason to support the expectation is that physical shops can receive online returns at staffed counters without disrupting ordinary sales.

utterances.speaker: Malik
utterances.text: But requiring every online customer to return purchases to a physical shop would be unfair to people who live far from shops.

utterances.speaker: Harriet
utterances.text: Nkechi, do you think that objection changes the case?

utterances.speaker: Nkechi
utterances.text: So you mean that physical shops can accept online returns at staffed counters without disrupting ordinary sales.

utterances.speaker: Harriet
utterances.text: In other words, Daniela wants customers to be expected to return online purchases to physical shops.

utterances.speaker: Selin
utterances.text: Shops already have staff and tills in place during their normal opening hours. Therefore, accepting online returns would not require every shop to open for longer hours.

utterances.speaker: Malik
utterances.text: Processing online returns takes shop workers' time. For that reason, online retailers should pay shops a fee for processing returned purchases.

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: A return kiosk can scan parcels and print receipts without requiring a sales assistant to handle every return. That is why retailers could make physical-shop returns efficient by installing return kiosks.

utterances.speaker: Selin
utterances.text: Customers can drop returned purchases at a shop while they are already visiting it for another reason. This makes a shop-return requirement less likely to create a separate journey for customers.

utterances.speaker: Nkechi
utterances.text: I once returned a pair of shoes to a shop during my lunch break.

utterances.speaker: Harriet
utterances.text: Before we close, should the policy include any safeguards for people who cannot easily reach a shop?

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: The consumer regulator's consultation on parcel returns closes on Friday.

spec.topic: Should schools let students choose their own start times within a daily attendance window?

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: Schools should let students choose their own start times within a daily attendance window, because that would let them match their arrival to their sleep needs.

utterances.speaker: Hamza
utterances.text: I disagree. Schools need a common start time to coordinate buses and family schedules.

utterances.speaker: Constance
utterances.text: So Esther is saying that students may select individual arrival times as long as they attend during the school day.

utterances.speaker: Hamza
utterances.text: As a side note, the school library is replacing its carpet during the summer holiday.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: Many teenagers' sleep needs conflict with the earliest fixed school start time, which supports my proposal because students need a way to avoid that conflict.

utterances.speaker: Constance
utterances.text: Staggered arrivals would spread demand on buses and nearby roads, because schools could then accommodate a flexible attendance window without adding buses. That is another reason to allow students to choose their start times.

utterances.speaker: Hamza
utterances.text: For an unrelated update, the school's chess club will hold its regional tournament in April.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: In other words, the proposal uses scheduling flexibility instead of requiring schools to expand their bus fleets. That makes the proposal workable because transport capacity would not have to grow.

utterances.speaker: Constance
utterances.text: A common attendance window can preserve each school's required amount of teaching time, and that supports letting students choose their own start times.

utterances.speaker: Rashid

utterances.speaker: Rashid

utterances.speaker: Bongani

utterances.speaker: Rashid

spec.topic: Should governments ban the release of genetically modified mosquitoes to control disease?

utterances.speaker: Aiko
utterances.text: Welcome to the programme. Tonight we ask whether governments should ban the release of genetically modified mosquitoes. Dalia, you first.

utterances.speaker: Dalia
utterances.text: Governments should not ban these releases, because trials in the Cayman Islands cut Aedes aegypti populations by more than 80 percent.

utterances.speaker: Aiko
utterances.text: So, Dalia, in other words, a ban would mean giving up a tool that works.

utterances.speaker: Helga
utterances.text: But releasing a modified species into the wild is irreversible; you cannot recall it.

utterances.speaker: Pablo
utterances.text: I should say that I am an entomologist at a university in Lima.

utterances.speaker: Pablo
utterances.text: Insecticide spraying alone is failing to stop dengue, since mosquitoes have developed resistance in many cities.

utterances.speaker: Helga
utterances.text: We know very little about the long-term effects on ecosystems, because the field trials have run for only a few years.

utterances.speaker: Aiko
utterances.text: Pablo, is there a safer way to do this?

utterances.speaker: Pablo
utterances.text: Releasing only male modified mosquitoes is safe for people, since male mosquitoes do not bite.

utterances.speaker: Aiko
utterances.text: So you are saying the insects released in these programmes cannot harm anyone through bites.

utterances.speaker: Dalia
utterances.text: Local communities should get a vote before any release, because they are the ones who live with the consequences.

utterances.speaker: Helga
utterances.text: Approval processes for these releases vary widely between countries.

utterances.speaker: Dalia
utterances.text: Put another way, Helga, there is no common safety standard for releasing modified mosquitoes.

utterances.speaker: Helga
utterances.text: Last year my own city had a dengue outbreak.

utterances.speaker: Aiko
utterances.text: Thank you all. That is all we have time for tonight.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: In other words, medicine sometimes cannot stop a dying patient's pain.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: Yes. Critics say vulnerable people would feel pressured to end their lives, but safeguards such as two independent doctors prevent that.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So you are saying that independent checks are enough to protect vulnerable people.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: That is shown by Oregon, which has had such safeguards since 1997 without evidence of widespread abuse. I say that because its yearly reports record almost no concerns about coercion.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Doctors' groups object, though: assisted dying is contrary to doctors' duty to do no harm, since several national medical associations oppose it.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: I think the right is justified precisely because the duty to do no harm includes a duty to relieve suffering, and the reason is that relief from suffering is what dying patients most ask of their doctors.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So, to put it plainly, you back a legal choice of assisted dying for terminally ill adults.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: Exactly, that is to say, the checks protect vulnerable people. My uncle died in a hospice last year.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there anything you would like to add?

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: Only that I have volunteered with a hospice charity for ten years.

utterances.speaker: Padraig

utterances.speaker: Odette

utterances.speaker: Malik

utterances.speaker: Gwen

utterances.speaker: Padraig

utterances.text: But mandatory canopy percentages can be unrealistic on constrained housing sites. That objection also challenges the case for a universal mandate.

utterances.speaker: Malik

utterances.speaker: Gwen

spec.topic: Should public schools provide free breakfast to every pupil, regardless of family income?

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Public schools should provide free breakfast to every pupil, regardless of family income, because a hungry pupil is less able to concentrate during morning lessons.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Another reason to make breakfast universal is that it removes the stigma attached to receiving help. I keep a chipped blue mug on my writing desk.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Critics claim that universal school breakfast would be too expensive. That objection is mistaken: universal breakfast can be funded within ordinary school meal budgets.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A further reason to adopt the policy is that free breakfast would improve pupils' readiness to learn. Another reason is that a universal program is simpler to administer than a means-tested program.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The policy would also give families more predictable support at the start of the school day, which supports providing breakfast to everyone. Schools can accommodate common dietary restrictions in a breakfast program, so this policy is practical.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Finally, providing breakfast at school would make reliable morning nutrition a shared public responsibility; that is why public schools should offer it to every pupil.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In other words, the proposal is to give every pupil breakfast at school rather than to limit assistance to pupils from low-income families.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Put differently, universal access makes breakfast ordinary for every pupil instead of marking some pupils as needy.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: To restate the administrative point, universal breakfast avoids the burden of checking pupils' family incomes.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: I usually write before sunrise.

utterances.speaker: Birgit

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: I support sealing in principle. A person who completes five crime-free years has demonstrated sustained law-abiding conduct, which is another reason for adopting the policy.

utterances.speaker: Jelena

utterances.speaker: Jelena
utterances.text: Employers and landlords do not always distinguish minor old offences from serious current risks; because of that, old minor records can create unfair barriers to employment and housing.

utterances.speaker: Joaquin

utterances.speaker: Rosalind
utterances.text: In other words, sealing old minor records is fair to people who have stayed crime-free, and that fairness supports automatic sealing.

utterances.speaker: Birgit
utterances.text: There is also an administrative question. Would the rule be workable?

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: Automatic sealing would give officials a simple and predictable rule to administer, which shows that the proposed sealing system would be straightforward to administer.

utterances.speaker: Rosalind

utterances.speaker: Jelena
utterances.text: In other words, five crime-free years is a reasonable threshold before a minor record is sealed; that is why the threshold should be adopted.

spec.topic: Should clinical trials be required to include equal numbers of all major demographic groups?

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: Welcome to the debate. Should clinical trials be required to include equal numbers of all major demographic groups?

utterances.speaker: Nkechi
utterances.text: Yes, clinical trials should be required to enroll equal numbers of all major demographic groups. I support that requirement because unequal enrollment can hide clinically important differences between groups.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: Xavier, is a fixed requirement workable in practice?

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: I disagree with the proposal because a strict equal-numbers requirement would make many clinical trials impractical.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: Equal enrollment gives investigators enough observations to compare treatment effects across demographic groups; that is a reason to require the rule.

utterances.speaker: Nkechi
utterances.text: Recruitment barriers already make some demographic groups less likely to join clinical trials, which is another reason to require equal enrollment.

utterances.speaker: Gideon
utterances.text: The hospital's ethics committee meets on the first Tuesday of every month.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: Xavier, what exactly would the rule require?

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: By equal numbers, the proposal means that every major demographic group would contribute the same number of participants.

utterances.speaker: Nkechi
utterances.text: Equal enrollment makes it harder for a treatment's harmful effects on a smaller group to go unnoticed, so that supports the requirement.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: In other words, Nkechi's proposal is a requirement for numerical parity among major demographic groups.

utterances.speaker: Gideon
utterances.text: Demographic groups can differ in how often they experience a disease and how they respond to treatment. Those differences are a reason to demand equal enrollment.

utterances.speaker: Gideon
utterances.text: The trial registry publishes study protocols before participant recruitment begins.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: Nkechi, give us your final argument for the policy.

utterances.speaker: Gideon
utterances.text: To restate Nkechi's position, she is calling for the same participant count from every major demographic group.

utterances.speaker: Nkechi
utterances.text: Equal enrollment would make the evidence more credible to patients who are often underrepresented, which supports making the requirement mandatory.

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: So you are saying that every major demographic group must have the same number of trial participants.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: The practical objection is clear. Soren, do you still support the requirement?

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: Yes. Equal enrollment is justified because medical evidence should apply reliably to the people who will use the treatment.
